body: At twenty to three the RAZR goes off on the nightstand in Danny’s room, rattling against the wood beside the lamp, and Jack has it in his fist before it can go twice. The outer screen says SKYE (MISFIT). It lights the crucifix over the door and the trophy on Danny’s shelf, the little gold man with his arm snapped off.

He takes it down the fourteen stairs barefoot, in the Carhartt over his pajama pants, and the seventh stair tells the house about it the way it always has. The house sleeps through it. His father is snoring in two parts behind the bedroom door; the lamp is off in the front room where Nonna sleeps in her chair. The phone stops on the stairs. It starts again in the kitchen. At the top of the basement steps, with the door pulled to behind him, he has two bars, which is where the house keeps them, and he opens it.
“No,” Jack says.

A party comes down the line from a long way off: a bass line, mostly, thudding through canvas. “You’re saying no to a *phone*, Jack,” Skye says. “It’s just me. I’m at the bottom of a driveway. The party’s at the top. I came down here where it’s only the car.”

He goes down in the dark to the bottom step and sits. The Dell is on where Gina left it on the card table, its fan whining, the screen saver throwing a slow blue drift across the paneling. Behind him the furnace lights with a thump and settles into its run. Ma’s laundry baskets, the old Zenith under a bedsheet, and in the laundry sink, under a dinner plate with a can of Contadina on it to keep it down, a slab of salt cod the size of a hymnal lying in water gone cloudy.
“Where are you?” she says. “Be specific.”
“The basement. The furnace. My sister’s computer.”
“What does it smell like?”
He breathes in, and regrets it. “Salt cod. Soaking.”
“Since when?”
“Monday.”
“Jack,” Skye says. “That’s a hostage situation.”
“My grandmother’s orders. My mother changes the water twice a day.”

“And it’s still in there. Breathing.” The bass thuds on. “I’m in a dress I can’t sit down in, so I’m lying across both seats with my shoes on the dashboard, in case you were picturing it. You were picturing it.” He was. “So,” she says. “A funny thing happened at a party.”

And she does a voice. A young man’s voice, unhurried, every vowel paid for in advance: *“I’m here strictly as a favor. There’s a woman named Pilar who does my mother’s eyebrows, and her nephew’s girlfriend went to Crossroads with the host, and Pilar said go, be seen, it’s Christmas — and I owe Pilar for a thing in 2006 that I can’t get into.”* After it, a little intake of air, held: the half second before the bow. Jack has watched it in doorways and dining rooms since August. He knows the voice before she says a name. He knows it from the eyebrows.
“Your roommate,” Skye says, herself again, “was being extremely odd tonight. Even for him.”
He hasn’t said a word. The furnace runs.
“I did your professor off a description,” she says. “I’ve had *years* of Ted.”
“Ted.”

“Ted. Theo, to you people. Since we were eleven.” The seat creaks under her. “His father’s company makes my show. Meridian — it’s at the end of every episode, after the caterer. Same sets. Same wrap parties. Every wrap party from sixth grade on, I was under the craft-services table with Ted, rating everybody’s outfits. We’re practically siblings. The bad kind. The kind who’ve seen each other at their worst.” A pause with bass in it. “I was sick on his shoes when I was fourteen and I will not be discussing it.”
“Do him,” she says. “You live with him. Say *strictly*.”
“I can’t do voices.”
“Everybody can do Ted. Say it.”
“Strictly,” Jack says.
“That’s a man buying a boat,” Skye says. “That’s a dentist buying a boat. Never do that again.”
“His father calls him Teddy.”
“I know,” Jack says. “I saw the card.”
“Then you know why I don’t. I’m the only one who calls him Ted.” Something rustles — her coat, the seat belt. “At the Hallorans’, I saw him walk in. With you. I got behind a ficus.”
“A ficus.”
“A big one. I’m a professional.”
In the den, with a Sharpie in her teeth, she had wanted to leave. “Too many people you went to middle school with,” he says.

“One,” Skye says. “Mostly one. And at Ellery — you told me your roommate asked why you looked like you’d been through a war. *Tell him it was a peace mission.* That was me waving at Ted over your head.” She doesn’t wait for him to ask the next part. “You want to know why I didn’t say. Because you’d have asked him about me. And he’d have told you the truth, and I wanted you to find it out slower.”
On the Dell twelve feet from where he’s sitting, the Sunday after Thanksgiving, it said *1 mutual friend: Theo Vance*, and he read it as Theo knowing everybody.

“Tonight,” she says, “I’m out on a terrace hiding from a hot tub, and he comes out through the slider, and he sees me, and he stops. He looks at me like he’s doing long division.” The voice again, lower, without the eyebrows in it: *“Callender. You’re in Marisol.”* Herself: “Since November.” Him: *“Since the Hallorans’.”*

“He had on the camel coat. It was fifty-five degrees on that terrace with a heat lamp going. Ted only wears a coat to a party he means to leave early, so he can leave holding something.” She clicks her tongue. “He wasn’t asking,” Skye says. “He knows, Jack. He’s known since your Thanksgiving. I friended you on a Wednesday, and Ted reads Facebook like it’s the trades and pretends he’s above it.” The seat creaks again; she’s sat up. “Here’s the part. Ted has never been careful with me in his life. He tells me I’ve got lipstick on my teeth in front of casting directors. He told me my first boyfriend looked like a thumb. Tonight he was careful. With every word. Ted’s only careful when he’s protecting somebody.”
She doesn’t say who.

“And then he goes,” and she’s him once more, the last of it: *“What are you doing, Callender?”* Herself: “I never know what I’m doing, Ted.” And Ted, gently, on his way back in through the slider: *“He does. That’s the problem.”*
Up at the top of the driveway somebody changes the song. She doesn’t add anything to it. In the laundry sink the plate on the baccalà ticks once against the porcelain as the furnace shakes the floor.

The bass through the canvas, and nothing over it — long enough that he takes the phone from his ear to see if he’s lost her. The little clock on the screen is still counting. When she comes back she’s close to the phone.
“I know,” Skye says. “I’m telling you now.”

response: “Did he do the bow?”
“From the *waist*,” Skye says. “On a terrace. To a girl he once watched throw up on his shoes. He held it, too. He held it like he was being graded.”

response: “Is he okay?”
She stops. He can hear the seat take her weight as she moves, and the turn signal ticking, which she must have knocked with her knee and doesn’t turn off.
“He’s Ted,” she says. Then: “No. But he never has been, with me. Don’t tell him I said so.”

response: “Okay.”
“Okay?”
“Okay.”
“You’re very hard to surprise,” Skye says.
“I’m sitting next to a fish.”

s08a.slug: WEDNESDAY · 3:00 AM · THE BASEMENT → THE SIDE YARD
body: “He’s coming here,” Jack says. “Christmas Eve. He called Monday and asked.”

Down the line something gets knocked — the gearshift, from the clunk of it. “To your *house*?” Skye says. “Oh, he’s going to be *so polite*. He’s going to bring your mother something in a box she’s afraid to open.”
“Balsamic. At Thanksgiving. In velvet.”
“Of *course* in velvet.” She’s rocking the car; the canvas creaks in its frame. “I would give a kidney to see Ted in a house where everybody shares a bathroom.”
“There’s a hook on the door.”
“Stop. Stop, I can’t.” She gets her breath back. “Eighteen days,” she says. “I’m not counting.”
“You said yes. I wrote it on my hand. It’s still there; I’m a terrible bather.”
Somebody comes down the driveway past her car, laughing, and goes back up. She waits for them to go.
“I’d rather be in your basement,” she says.
“It smells like fish.”
“Then I’d rather be in your basement with you in it.”

The furnace cuts out. In the quiet the Dell’s fan sounds like a small plane. He sits on the bottom step with the phone against his ear and the concrete under his heels, and doesn’t have anything smart to say. On her end, nothing either; the bass, and her breathing.
“Is it snowing there?” she says.
“It snowed Saturday.”
“So there’s snow.”
“There’s old snow.”
“Are you wearing shoes?”
“No.”
“Good. Don’t. Go stand in it.” And when he laughs: “I’m serious. Go outside and do the weather. Like the girl on the eleven o’clock. You have a girl on the eleven o’clock.”
“Everybody has a girl on the eleven o’clock.”
“Then be her. Go.”

He goes. Up the basement steps, across the kitchen linoleum in the dark, and out the side door, and the spring takes the door out of his hand and slams it behind him like a shot, loud enough for every house on Glenwood Avenue, and he stands on the step with the phone at his ear, waiting for a light to come on upstairs. None does.

The side yard is three days of snow gone hard on top, gray at the edges where the plow threw the street up onto it. The first step holds him. The second goes through the crust to the ankle, and both feet are on fire at once, and then they’re just gone, which is easier. Frank’s blue lights are wound around the tub at the back of the yard, and the Madonna stands in it with the snow on her gone to a crust, the lights making her blue all the way up.
“Five-day,” Skye says. “Give me a high. Point at something.”

He points at the Madonna. “Good morning,” he says. “It’s five past three on Glenwood Avenue. Here at the Costigan station the Blessed Mother is reporting three days of accumulation, holding steady, under blue lights.”
“Turn to camera. Smile like you’re paid.”
He turns to camera, which is the neighbors’ garage. “Two doors up, an inflatable Santa remains on his face. Three days. No change in his condition.”
“Hand out. Show me a front.”

He shows her a front. Out of the dryer vent by the side door the furnace’s breath comes up white and rolls off along the siding, and he puts it in the forecast. He sweeps his free arm from the neighbors’ to the alley pole. “Thursday, clear. A high in the thirties. Christmas, I can’t help you with Christmas. Christmas is out of my hands.” He looks up, where the moon would be. “And no moon tonight, folks. None at all. Somebody took it.”
“Do the Madonna,” Skye says. “From the top. I fell asleep before you finished her.”

“My grandfather dug her in before I was born. A clawfoot tub, on its end, painted blue inside. She’s concrete. She weighs more than my father.” He points, weather-girl, at the blue. “Light accumulation in both hands.”

Skye is laughing so hard the horn goes off at her end, a short honk at the bottom of a driveway in the hills, and she says *sorry, sorry* to whoever’s up there, and keeps laughing. And so is he, barefoot to the shins in old snow in his pajama pants at five past three in the morning, with his breath going up in the alley light and one arm out showing a girl in California a cold front over Brownlee Woods, laughing so his ribs hurt and he has to bend over his knees, and nothing in him wants to be anywhere but here.
“Go to bed, Ohio,” Skye says when she can. “Next time I call, it isn’t going to be about Ted.”
She hangs up.
On the kitchen linoleum his feet are red to the ankle.
Wednesday the light goes off Glenwood a little before five. At six Ma is down at the laundry sink giving the baccalà its last water, and Jack is on the top step with the RAZR, where the bars are.

body: The upstairs bathroom is the only door in the house with a lock: a hook and an eye Frank screwed into the frame in 1998, the year Gina learned doorknobs. The radiator under the window knocks and hisses. On the bar hang Ma’s guest towels, white, a gold *C* stitched in the corner of each, which are for looking at. His good coat for Midnight Mass is on the hook on the back of the door.

Out in the house everybody is getting ready for church at once: Gina has the hair dryer going in Ma and Pop’s room on the long cord, Rosie is being talked into tights, and somewhere downstairs Nonna is teaching Theo, in Italian, to tie a tie he has been tying since he was six.

Jack drops the hook into the eye. On the RAZR’s outer screen the little envelope is waiting, where it has been since the fish. He opens the phone. The message is at the top of the inbox, a small picture icon and a line of lowercase under it.

body.text: *Picture Msg* · the parrot is scandalized. you should be too. merry christmas eve ohio

choices.key: Christmas Eve, behind the bathroom’s hook-and-eye, you opened the picture Skye sent and answered it.
response: He opens it. *Retrieving.* It comes down the little screen in stripes, one band at a time from the top, and he tilts the phone up to the bulb over the mirror and puts his back flat against the door, against the hook. White first: a tree, flocked so heavy with fake snow its branches look upholstered — her mother’s, it has to be — and a slice of gray couch, and carpet. At the edge of the frame, the parrot on its perch, green, one eye turned on the camera like a chaperone. Then her.

She’s lying on the carpet under the tree, and the picture is taken from straight above: her arm up out of the frame, the phone held high over her and pointed down, blind. The lens is where a man would be if he were leaning over her. Her hair is spread out on the carpet in the tree’s shadow. She has nothing on but a strand of the tree’s white lights, wound around her loosely, once over a shoulder and down across her and around one hip, and the small bulbs lie on her skin and light it where they lie and leave the rest of her to the dim of the room. She’s looking up at the lens with her lower lip caught in her teeth, a laugh coming up in her that she hasn’t let out yet — at the lights, at the parrot, at her own production values.
He stands against the door a while with his heart going. He answers her, and what he sends is true.

s16b.slug: FRIDAY · 9:40 AM · THE FRONT PORCH, THE GLIDER

body.text: WHO. HOW. calling at 640 my time. dont go anywhere

body: It rains all morning. It comes down on the porch roof in a long hush and off the gutters in strings, and the old snow in the yards has gone gray and is shrinking into the gutters as he watches. Jack has the tarp pulled back off the glider and Nonna’s afghan over his knees. At 9:40 the RAZR goes.
“Are you on the glider?” Skye says.
“Under the tarp.”

“Good. Stay there.” She’s on her mother’s balcony in Studio City; there’s traffic on a big road somewhere below her and, close to the phone, a bird clearing its throat. “That’s the parrot. It says *momager*. It says *Merry Christmas* now too — my mother taught it for the network party. Now. Who. How. Everything. In order. Don’t skip, I’ll know.”

So he gives it to her in order. Gina’s present, wrapped in the *Vindicator*’s funnies; Rosie handing it to him in front of everybody before Gina could get to her; the box set; the Post-it. The front window behind him is full of his family pretending to do something else: Gina at the glass with her arms crossed, Rosie with her nose on it, his mother behind them with the curtain in her hand, and Theo at the back, in the new Browns hat, reading the DVD box.
“And my grandmother points at the cover,” he says, “and says *L’attrice!*”
“She *pointed*?”
“At the girl in the middle. In the blazer.”
“That’s season two,” Skye says. “I was eighteen and they had me in a blazer with *shoulder pads*. Keep going.”

The Dell on its extension cord on the kitchen table. Gina, four minutes, her own account. The fan page — Brazil. The boat. Nonna with her rosary out, saying things in Calabrese that Gina wouldn’t translate. His father, who looked at the screen for a long time and then said: “Huh.”
“That’s a *rave*,” Skye says. “That’s four stars. I’m putting it on the poster. Wave at them.”
“No.”
“Wave at them, Jack.”
He turns around on the glider and waves at the window. Gina waves back. Rosie waves with both hands. His mother lets the curtain drop.
“What did your mother say? Don’t give me the gist. Give me the line.”

He tells her: Ma at the sink, with her back to the room and the water running. *Is she Catholic, at least?* He tries to tell her how it sounds — the flat Valley *a*’s, the *at least* coming down on the end of it like the lid on a pot.
Skye is quiet for about as long as it takes to try it in her mouth. And she does it. “*Is she Catholic, at least?*”
It’s near enough that he looks over his shoulder at the window.

“Jack.” She’s starting to go. “Jack. They know me as the *nice* one. I’m on a boat in a bikini on the kitchen table and your grandmother’s praying the rosary at me, and it says on the DVD that I’m the NICE one. They think I’m *Cassidy*.” And she’s gone: she’s put the phone down on the balcony rail to laugh, and he can hear her a little way off from it, helpless, and the parrot, much closer, says something into the mouthpiece in a language of its own. When she picks it up again she’s out of breath. “I’m having it put on my headstone. *Here lies the nice one.*”
The rain comes harder for a minute and lets up.
“Your mother didn’t ask if I’m Catholic,” Skye says. “She asked if you still are.”
He doesn’t have anything ready for that. He looks at the street, the water running in the gutter toward Market, the Santa two doors up lying in a puddle now instead of a drift.
“I’d like to be in that kitchen,” she says. “Your grandmother would hate me. I’d win her by Easter.”

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Made me answer the question I couldn’t at the Starlite. Thursday at one in the morning, no moon at all, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook. Christmas week: Theo’s known her since they were eleven — his father’s company makes her show. She calls him Ted; nobody else does. She saw us walk into the Hallorans’ together and hid behind a ficus. “Peace mission” was for him. He ran into her at a party in the hills on the twenty-second, and she says he knows. She had me do the weather barefoot in the snow. Eighteen days; she’s not counting. Christmas morning my family found her — Gina gave me her show on DVD. They know her as the nice one. She wants it on her headstone.

response: “They’re scared of you,” he says.

The parrot fills the gap. Then: “Good,” Skye says. “I’m scared of them.” And straight on from it she wants to know what Nonna said in Calabrese, exactly, and whether Gina translated, and he tells her Gina refused.

Behind her the parrot says *Merry Christmas* in her mother’s network voice, and somebody inside calls her name. “That’s my mother. There’s a hotel, and a brunch, and the omelet man is expecting me.” She stops at the door; the slider rumbles in its track. “Merry Christmas, Ohio. Tell Ted the girl he was careful with says hi.”

She’s gone. The rain comes off the end of the gutter in a rope and spatters the steps. Jack sits on the glider with the phone shut in his hand and Nonna’s afghan over his knees and his family behind the glass at his back, and laughs by himself on the front porch in the rain on Christmas morning — at the parrot, at the headstone, at the Santa in his puddle.
